name: Levothyroxine (T4)
lead: Levothyroxine is a synthetic form of thyroxine (T4), the main hormone made by the thyroid gland. It is the standard replacement therapy for hypothyroidism and is also used to suppress TSH in some thyroid cancers.[1][2][3] Hypothyroidism can show up in how a person looks: dry coarse skin, hair loss, puffiness and swelling around the eyes are listed among its signs, alongside weight gain and fatigue, and treatment aims to restore normal thyroid function.[8][9][18][21]

The route by which levothyroxine can matter for appearance is therefore corrective: when a thyroid deficiency is present and treated, the body's metabolism and energy return toward normal, which can affect body weight, energy for training and general well-being. Because excess thyroid hormone causes weight loss, levothyroxine has also been misused for slimming. The US label carries a boxed warning that it should not be used to treat obesity or for weight loss, stating that doses within normal replacement ranges are ineffective for weight reduction in euthyroid patients and larger doses may cause serious toxicity.[3]

On looksmaxxing forums it is discussed mainly by people who suspect or have borderline thyroid abnormalities, sometimes alongside growth hormone, and by teenagers asking what it could do for height or looks.[7][15] Replies in those threads frequently state that it treats hypothyroidism and does nothing for looks otherwise.[15] No trials have examined it as an appearance treatment in people with normal thyroid function.

It is one of the most prescribed medicines in the United States, with over 80 million prescriptions in 2023 and 2024, and it is on the WHO List of Essential Medicines.[4] In looksmaxxing and wider hormone-optimisation circles it sits next to related products such as liothyronine (T3) and desiccated thyroid extract, which clinicians' guidelines generally do not favor over levothyroxine.[19][20]

paras: Levothyroxine treats primary, secondary and tertiary hypothyroidism, including congenital forms, and is used for TSH suppression in differentiated thyroid cancer.[3][2][4] A 2024 Lancet review describes levothyroxine monotherapy as the standard treatment, one that restores thyroid function tests to the reference range and improves symptoms in most patients.[8] Hashimoto thyroiditis is the cause of primary hypothyroidism in up to 85% of patients in iodine-sufficient regions.[9] Guidelines from the American Thyroid Association address its dosing and the dissatisfaction some patients report on monotherapy.[5] Treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism is debated.[6][4]

Reviews list weight gain (reported in roughly a quarter to well over half of patients), fatigue and cognitive complaints among the features of hypothyroidism, and the label notes that under-replacement tends to go with weight gain while over-replacement tends to go with weight loss.[9][3] People who describe looks-related goals on forums are usually referring to this link between thyroid status, weight and energy.[7]

Reviews of the skin in thyroid disease describe dry skin, hair shedding and nail changes among hypothyroid findings, and note that cutaneous signs can be among the first indicators of thyroid imbalance.[21][22] Wikipedia lists dry coarse skin, hair loss, puffiness and an expressionless face with swelling around the eyes among appearance-related signs.[18] In these patients, replacement therapy is the treatment aimed at the underlying deficiency, which is the context in which appearance changes are discussed.

Subclinical hypothyroidism means a raised TSH with normal T4. It is common, particularly in older adults and women, and Wikipedia reports that treatment generally is not beneficial in non-pregnant people unless TSH is quite high, though guidelines vary.[18][6] The TRUST trial in older adults found no symptom or tiredness improvement over placebo.[14]

T4 is converted in peripheral tissues to the more active T3, which binds nuclear receptors and regulates gene transcription and protein synthesis; about 80% of T3 comes from T4 deiodination.[3] Oral absorption is 40 to 80%, the half-life is about a week, and steady state takes roughly six weeks, so changes are assessed after several weeks of testing with TSH and free T4.[4][1] Absorption is reduced by calcium, iron, fibre, soy, coffee and certain antacids, and labels advise taking it on an empty stomach apart from food.[4][3]

Sheep thyroid extract was introduced for myxoedema in 1891 by George Redmayne Murray, and desiccated thyroid was in use through the early twentieth century.[18][19] Thyroxine was first isolated in pure form in 1914 at the Mayo Clinic by Edward Calvin Kendall and synthesised in 1927 by Charles Harington and George Barger.[4] Synthetic levothyroxine came into US clinical practice in the late 1940s and replaced thyroid extracts gradually; by the 1980s more patients received synthetic products than desiccated extract.[1][19] The TSH radioimmunoassay of 1971 became the most specific marker of thyroid status.[18] A Nature Reviews Endocrinology piece dates the supersession of extract by levothyroxine to the 1970s and notes no major treatment innovation since.[11]

In the US, FDA approved generic versions as interchangeable in 2004; the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists, the Endocrine Society and the American Thyroid Association disagreed that formulations were bioequivalent and advised patients to stay on one formulation and recheck TSH after a switch.[4]

In hypothyroidism, levothyroxine normalises TSH in most adults when dosed and absorbed properly, but a minority remain symptomatic despite normal TSH.[10] A review in Nature Reviews Endocrinology reports that replacement improves but does not always normalise quality of life, particularly in mild hypothyroidism, and that combination or desiccated-extract therapies have not shown robust gains in patient satisfaction.[11] Absorption is reduced by calcium, iron and fibre, and some drugs and gut conditions interfere with it.[4][3]

Liothyronine is synthetic T3, approved in 1956, with a faster onset and shorter half-life than levothyroxine; its US label carries the same boxed warning about use for obesity.[20] Desiccated thyroid extract is dried porcine thyroid (brands include Armour Thyroid and NP Thyroid) containing roughly a 4:1 ratio of T4 to T3 compared with about 11:1 in humans; the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and the Royal College of Physicians recommend against its use for hypothyroidism, citing superphysiological T3 levels and the lack of long-term randomised data.[19] Wikipedia also reports that adding T3 or using extract is not well supported and most major guidelines discourage them.[18] A randomised double-blind crossover study of 75 hypothyroid patients compared levothyroxine, desiccated extract and combination therapy.[13]

sections.h: Adverse effects and the weight-loss warning
paras: Adverse reactions are mainly those of overtreatment: weight loss, heat intolerance, sweating, anxiety, insomnia, tremor, palpitations and arrhythmias. Long-term TSH suppression has been linked to cardiac problems and reduced bone density, and it is contraindicated in thyrotoxicosis, acute myocardial infarction and uncorrected adrenal insufficiency.[3][4] The label warns of cardiac risk in older people and in those with heart disease, and says the boxed warning is especially relevant when thyroid hormone is combined with sympathomimetic appetite suppressants.[3]

The US label's boxed warning states that thyroid hormones, including levothyroxine, should not be used for the treatment of obesity or for weight loss, because replacement-range doses are ineffective in euthyroid patients and larger doses may produce serious or even life-threatening toxicity.[3] Liothyronine carries the same warning.[20] Poor adherence is the most common cause of elevated TSH in people on appropriate doses, and over-suppression over the long term is associated with cardiac effects and reduced bone density.[4]

Levothyroxine is prescription-only in the US, Canada and Australia, and is among the most widely prescribed medicines in the United States.[4][1] Brand names include Synthroid, Levoxyl, Euthyrox, Unithroid and Tirosint.[4]

Forum posts show users posting TSH and free T4 values that sit at the edge of the reference range and discussing self-prescribing levothyroxine, sometimes in combination with growth hormone.[7] Other threads ask whether it will help height, weight or appearance; replies commonly say it treats hypothyroidism only.[15] One thread asks about taking a relative's supply, with replies joking about height gains.[16] On T Nation, posts mention levothyroxine mostly in the context of users who are prescribed it alongside testosterone therapy, and one user describes titrating toward a low-normal TSH and high-normal free T4.[17] The communities' discussion thus mixes people with diagnosed thyroid disease, people interpreting borderline bloodwork, and people looking for a physique or height edge.

Trials of levothyroxine concern hypothyroidism, congenital hypothyroidism, pregnancy, thyroid cancer and bioequivalence of formulations; guidelines and reviews summarise them.[5][6] In the TRUST trial, older adults with subclinical hypothyroidism who received levothyroxine did not show improved symptoms or tiredness scores over the study period compared with placebo.[14] A randomised, double-blind crossover study of 75 hypothyroid patients compared levothyroxine, desiccated thyroid extract and levothyroxine plus liothyronine.[13] A 2026 randomised trial of 88 adults with well-controlled hypothyroidism compared fasting intake with breakfast intake with a dose increase and found comparable TSH stability between groups.[12] Studies in euthyroid people for cosmetic purposes were not found. The label states that euthyroid patients do not lose weight on replacement doses.[3]

lore.intro: Levothyroxine is discussed on looksmaxxing forums mainly in relation to thyroid bloodwork, hormone optimisation stacks and, occasionally, height or weight hopes.[7][15]

claims.claim: Low-normal thyroid levels can be corrected with levothyroxine to improve how people look and feel.
claims.believers: Some forum users post their own TSH and fT4 values and describe self-managed use of levothyroxine alongside growth hormone.[7]
claims.experts: Guidelines support treatment of overt hypothyroidism, while treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism is debated, and no studies examine appearance outcomes in euthyroid people.[5][6] In older adults with subclinical hypothyroidism, a randomised trial did not find symptom improvement.[14]

claims.claim: A teenager who is still growing and has hypothyroid-like symptoms may gain looks or height from starting it.
claims.believers: A forum poster in his teens with a brother who has hypothyroidism asks what levothyroxine would do for his appearance, expecting he may be hypothyroid too.[15]
claims.experts: Replies in that thread say it helps hypothyroidism only, and the label describes replacement therapy for diagnosed deficiency.[15][3]

claims.claim: Levothyroxine can be used to lose weight.
claims.believers: Weight loss is a recognised effect of excess thyroid hormone, which is why it has been misused for slimming.[3]
claims.experts: The US label has a boxed warning against use for obesity or weight loss, saying normal replacement doses are ineffective in euthyroid patients and larger doses may be life-threatening.[3]

claims.claim: Desiccated thyroid or added T3 feels better and keeps people leaner than T4 alone
claims.believers: Proponents of natural thyroid products say they relieve symptoms that persist in some patients despite a normal TSH on levothyroxine.
claims.experts: The American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and Royal College of Physicians recommend against extract, and a review reports combination therapies have not shown robust gains in satisfaction.[19][11]

claims.claim: Hypothyroid features such as puffiness, dry skin and hair shedding can resolve after treatment
claims.believers: Patients and clinicians describe skin, hair and puffiness changes as part of the hypothyroid picture that treatment of the deficiency is meant to address.[18]
claims.experts: Dermatology reviews describe these skin and hair signs as thyroid-related findings in hypothyroidism, with treatment of the underlying deficiency the approach.[21][22]

card.summary: The standard hypothyroidism drug, which carries a boxed warning against use for weight loss.
card.note: Boxed warning: not for obesity or weight loss; excess doses can cause serious cardiac effects.

quick.overview:
Levothyroxine is synthetic T4, prescribed for hypothyroidism and some thyroid cancers.

It is sometimes discussed on forums in connection with weight and hormone optimisation, though no trial supports an appearance use in people with normal thyroid function.
quick.mechanism: It is converted to T3, which binds thyroid hormone receptors and regulates gene transcription and metabolism.
quick.risks: Overdose causes hyperthyroid symptoms including arrhythmia and bone loss. The label warns against use for weight loss, and it is prescription-only.

chain: Metabolic rate and energy move toward normal
Easier weight management and training capacity
angle.text: For someone with diagnosed hypothyroidism, replacing the missing hormone addresses a documented cause of weight gain and fatigue, which can change body composition and the energy available for training.[8][9] People with normal thyroid function are not expected to gain an appearance benefit, and the label warns against using it for weight loss.[3]
